clinicalPearls: Pseudochylothorax is a cholesterol-rich, lipid-laden pleural effusion that looks milky or turbid but arises from chronic pleural inflammation rather than thoracic duct disruption.
It classically develops in long-standing effusions (often present for years) with markedly thickened, fibrotic or calcified pleura.
The two commonest causes are chronic tuberculous pleuritis and rheumatoid pleuritis; historical artificial (therapeutic) pneumothorax is another.
It is distinguished from true chylothorax biochemically: pseudochylothorax has high cholesterol (typically markedly elevated) and/or cholesterol crystals, with low triglycerides and no chylomicrons.
True chylothorax, by contrast, has high triglycerides and chylomicrons and reflects a thoracic duct leak.
Cholesterol crystals appear as rhomboid, notched plates on polarised light microscopy of the fluid.
Many patients are relatively asymptomatic despite turbid fluid, with symptoms determined by the underlying disease and any trapped lung.
Management targets the underlying cause, with therapeutic aspiration for symptoms and decortication reserved for trapped lung or persistent symptomatic effusion.
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudochylothorax develops when a pleural effusion persists for a prolonged period within a thickened, poorly reabsorbing pleural space. Chronic inflammation and slow fluid turnover lead to accumulation of cholesterol and lecithin-globulin complexes, probably derived from degenerating red and white cells, within the trapped fluid. The fibrotic pleura impairs lipid clearance, so cholesterol concentrates and may crystallise, producing the characteristic opalescent, turbid appearance. Because the retained lipid is cholesterol rather than triglyceride-rich chyle, the thoracic duct is intact, which is the key distinction from chylothorax.
additionalDifferentials: Empyema (may also appear turbid or milky)
Rheumatoid or other connective tissue disease effusion
additionalInvestigations: Pleural fluid cholesterol and triglyceride levels
Pleural fluid microscopy for cholesterol crystals and lipoprotein analysis for chylomicrons
Pleural fluid cell count, protein, LDH, glucose and pH (Light's criteria)
Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase and mycobacterial culture for tuberculosis
Rheumatoid factor and connective tissue serology
CT thorax to assess pleural thickening, calcification and trapped lung
Pleural biopsy where the underlying cause remains unclear
redFlags: Features suggesting active tuberculosis (fever, weight loss) requiring treatment
A new or enlarging pleural mass raising concern for malignancy
Signs of superimposed empyema or sepsis
Progressive breathlessness from a trapped, non-expandable lung
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign and its outlook is dictated by the underlying disease; the effusion itself is chronic and often stable, though a trapped lung may cause persistent breathlessness that requires decortication.
pitfalls: Confusing pseudochylothorax with true chylothorax and pursuing an unnecessary search for thoracic duct injury.
Assuming turbid fluid always represents empyema.
Overlooking underlying tuberculosis or rheumatoid disease that needs specific treatment.
Repeatedly aspirating a trapped lung without addressing the underlying pleural thickening.
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Treat the underlying cause, giving anti-tuberculous chemotherapy for chronic tuberculous pleuritis or optimising disease-modifying therapy for rheumatoid pleuritis
Therapeutic pleural aspiration or drainage to relieve breathlessness in symptomatic effusions
Conservative monitoring for stable, minimally symptomatic chronic effusions
Decortication for a trapped lung causing persistent dyspnoea, with thoracic surgery referral
Recognise and account for any historical iatrogenic cause such as prior artificial pneumothorax
Respiratory follow-up with monitoring of the underlying disease and lung function
